message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
## Tomorrow's route

**The only order that works is B → A → C.** It meets every constraint, but it gets the van back to the depot at **exactly 12:00, with no slack at all.**

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive **B** (20 min drive) |
| 08:50–09:05 | Unload at B. Done before the shop opens at 09:30 ✓ |
| 09:05–09:30 | Drive B → A (25 min) |
| 09:30–09:45 | Unload at **A**, inside the 09:00–10:00 window ✓ |
| 09:45–10:25 | Drive A → C (40 min) |
| 10:25–10:55 | **Break (30 min)**, taken while waiting for C to open to deliveries ✓ |
| 11:00–11:15 | Unload at **C**, at the earliest time they'll accept ✓ |
| 11:15–12:00 | Drive C → depot (45 min) |
| **12:00** | **Back at depot** ✓ (exactly on the deadline) |

### Why no other order works

- **B has to come before A.** If the driver does A first, the earliest he can unload is 09:00, so he finishes at 09:15 and reaches B at 09:40. That's after the shop opens.
- **C has to come last.** It won't accept anything before 11:00, and B and A both have to be done well before that.

### The tight finish

The 12:00 return depends entirely on C. Unloading there can't start before 11:00 and takes 15 minutes, and the drive back takes 45. Nothing can be done earlier to create slack. If C keeps the driver waiting even a few minutes, he'll be back late.

Options:
- Ask C whether the driver can start unloading at **10:45**. That gives 15 minutes of margin, and the break still fits (10:15–10:45 if he gets there earlier, or shorten the wait).
- Check whether "back by 12:00" is a hard limit.
- Make sure C has someone ready to receive at 11:00 sharp.

This also assumes the drive from C back to the depot takes the same 45 minutes as the outbound trip.

## Van name ideas

- **Chester Drawers**
- **The Sideboard Express**
- **Vanity Unit**
- **Restoration Rover**
- **Dovetail**

## Friendlier "on the way" text

> Hi [Name], your driver from [Business] is on the way and should be with you in about [X] minutes. Please make sure someone's home to receive your furniture. See you soon!

## Evening-before text (142 characters)

> Hi Sarah, your furniture from Hale Restorations arrives tomorrow 9-10am. We'll text when the driver's on the way. Questions? Call 01234 567890

That example comes to **142 characters**. Long customer or business names will push it up, so keep the whole message under 160.

Two things that can split it into two texts even under 160:
- **Emoji.**
- **Curly apostrophes.** Some phones and texting tools convert straight apostrophes to curly ones automatically. Either of these switches the message to a format with a 70-character limit. Send a test text to check.

## Three checks before handing furniture over

1. **Condition:** no new scratches, dents or knocks from the journey. Compare against photos taken at the workshop if you have them.
2. **Completeness:** it's the right item, with all parts included, such as shelves, drawers, keys, handles and any fittings.
3. **Function:** drawers and doors open smoothly, legs are secure, and the piece stands level and steady where it's placed.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Emailed, with the customer signing on a phone or tablet at the door.** It's harder to lose, can include photos of the item as delivered, and is easy to find if there's a dispute later. Keep a few paper notes in the van for when there's no signal, or for customers who prefer paper.

## Proof of delivery

> **Proof of delivery** is the record showing the item was delivered to the right person and address, when, and in what condition. It's usually a signature, printed name, time and a photo.
